actions.reason: Target was encode_ir. I tried replacing the per-group divmod(i, big) in b58encode's main loop with `i % big` and `i //= big`, which removes the builtin call and the result tuple. Outputs were identical, but every metric got worse: encode_ir ratio 1.0517 (217807362 to 229075196), decode_ir 1.0218, check_ir 1.0088. Running a second pass over the big integer costs more than the divmod call it saves. I reverted the edit, so the working tree matches the parent. Earlier attempts on this tip also stayed under the 1% minimum: import trimming, loop unrolling and the decode lane merge. The other options I considered are expected rather than measured gains. Larger digit groups or a bigger lookup table would cost more in table building or small-int operations than they save. Divide-and-conquer splitting moves work into multi-limb division, which is likely more expensive here. Converting groups into digits in parallel across fixed-width lanes needs exact reciprocal arithmetic and too large a diff to fit the remaining budget safely. Stopping without a candidate.

journal.text:
Test agent here. Target was encode_ir in base58/__init__.py. I replaced the per-group divmod(i, big) in b58encode's main loop with i % big and i //= big. The idea was to skip the builtin call and the result tuple. Same bytes out was the bar.

Measured: outputs were identical. Every metric got worse. encode_ir went from 217807362 to 229075196, ratio 1.0517 against a required 0.9900. decode_ir ratio 1.0218. check_ir ratio 1.0088. Outcome: rejected, no improvement. I reverted the edit and submitted nothing.

What I believe now: divmod is not the waste here. Splitting it means two passes over the big integer per group. That costs more than the call it saves. The loop already batches digits per divmod, so the cheap trick is spent.

Next I will reread the encode loop for work outside the big-int math. That means the per-char alphabet lookup, the leading zero count and the final join. I will count the steps per output char before I touch anything.
